content:
Get urgent help

Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 for a suddenly very painful joint, swelling, skin colour change, difficulty moving it, or joint pain with feeling unwell, fever or shivering. Septic arthritis is a joint infection needing prompt treatment. Fever is not always present, so do not wait for it.

When to call 999

Call 999 or go to A&E if you think someone has sepsis with signs such as confusion or slurred speech, severe breathlessness or very fast breathing, or blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin. A rash that does not fade under a glass is another emergency sign. Do not wait for every symptom, and do not drive yourself to A&E.

Why prompt assessment matters

Symptoms can develop quickly. Gout, injury and other illnesses may also cause a hot or swollen joint, but you cannot reliably distinguish them at home. Explain when symptoms started and whether you have a joint replacement, recent surgery, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis or medicines that affect immunity.

What treatment may involve

People with septic arthritis are usually treated in hospital. Treatment may include antibiotics into a vein and drainage of fluid from the joint, followed by antibiotic tablets. The team decides which tests and procedures are needed. Finish prescribed antibiotics for the duration you are told, even if symptoms improve.

After hospital treatment

Follow the discharge and follow-up plan. Physiotherapy may help movement return as recovery allows. A joint replacement infection can need a different surgical plan. Seek advice promptly if you worsen or symptoms return rather than relying on an expected recovery timetable.
